But that information relates to the Ottawa buildings, while this item is for coal for public buildings throughout the Dominion.
I think that if the hon. minister could give us an account of the coal bought in the different towns, and the prices paid, that information would be valuable.
I shall be very pleased to bring down a return showing the amount used in the different towns. Of course, I cannot be expected to have that here.
No.

Sly hon. friend from West Toronto (Sir. Clarke), who is not present at the moment, informed me at six o'clock, as I understood him, that there was some information to be brought down with regard to this.

No, there were two other items which the hon. member (Sir. Clarke) asked to have stand until the information was furnished. I have a statement here which I will hand to him, and the other statement which he asked for will be laid on the Table tomorrow. The officials of the department could not get it ready to-day.
Could the hon. minister give me the figures showing the quantity of coal for the government building at "St. Thomas, the price and name of the contractor ?

I am not able to give the prices of each place, but, as I have said, I shall be pleased to bring down a return giving that information.
Lighting Dominion public buildings, $75,000.
There is a very large increase here.
It is a marked improvement in the system to bring the expenditures down all in one item. We may conclude, therefore, that so far as this item is concerned, there will be no further vote asked.

Not with regard to this item. The object of the department will be to make a correct estimate of what will be required. The difference between the vote of $55,000 and what will be required will have to be brought down under a new estimate, but there will be no supplementary estimate for 1903-4. This is estimated to cover the full amount.
The supplementary estimate to which the hon. gentleman refers has yet to be brought down for this year to cover the shortage of the current year.

That has been the practice. But henceforth we are going to take an appropriation for the full amount required.
Water-Dominion public buildings, $16,000.
Does this cover the water tax in cities for water supplied to government buildings ?

It is to supply water to the various public buildings under the control of the Dominion government. The officers of the department think that $16,000 will be sufficient. We had a small balance left over last year, when the sum was $16,000, the same as this year.
Electric and other power for running elevators, stamp cancelling machines, &c., Dominion public buildings, $8,000.

Electricity is used in the Montreal post of-Mr. INGRAM.
flee for stamp cancelling machines, freight and passenger elevators, $3,200 ; stamp cancelling machine in Quebec post office, $200 ; Toronto, elevator at the station in connection with the post office, stamp cancelling machine at the post office, elevator at the custom house, amounting altogether to $950; Ottawa, one elevator in the east block, two in the parliament building, one at the military stores, current for the fire pump, stamp cancelling machine in the post office, $2,270; Victoria, B.C., passenger and freight elevator, $920 ; Vancouver, stamp cancelling machine at post office.
Could the minister tell us what it costs to run the elevator in the Sey-hold building ?
That is not run by electricity. These items I have read represent the cost of electrical power.
Did we not have a power house at the foot of the hill here a few years ago ? What was done with that ?

The machinery became obsolete and the plant was abandoned. The machinery is still there.
Harbours and river, Nova Seotia-Amagandus wharf, $2,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the minister please explain where in the Auditor General's Report we will find the details of the expenditure at this place ?
None of the money voted was spent last year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then why should you ask for a vote this year ? I see that it has been voted for two years and nothing done. Perhaps, if it is not necessary, you might drop the item.

In explanation I may say that it is quite right that this money has not been spent though previously voted, but the work is now under way. It is being done by day's labour, and it is intended to spend $1,000 during the current year, so that, we are revoting $1,000 and asking for $2,000 more as it is estimated that the cost of this work will be $4,000.
What purpose is to be served by this wharf ?

I find that this wharf is being built for the local trade principally. From the petition presented by the inhabitants of this district there are considerable shipments of' fire wood and coal from this point. As other wharfs are a good distance from this place and the roads are very bad it was thought desirable in the public interest to serve these people by building this wharf.
Is it a new wharf ?
Yes.
When was this money expended on this wharf ?
The work is under way now. It is expected that $1,000 will he spent before the 30th June. We are asking for a revote of a $1,000 and $2,000 more to complete the work.
What will be the depth of the water when the wharf is completed ?

I am sorry I cannot give the hon. gentleman the information he asks for.
Mr. INGRAM, The Auditor General's Report does not show any expenditure on this work.
No, none of this money was spent last year.
So that the benefit will be from the landing of coal ?
Coal and fire wood seems to be principally shipped from that point.
Does the department purchase the land or how do you secure it before commencing the construction of a wharf like this ?

In this case the proprietor of the land at the foot of the road where the wharf is to be built has made a free grant to the Crown of the site.
Mr, BLAIN. Is there any population in this town, or village ?
This is just a scattered settlement along the coast of Cape Breton.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What is the expected revenue from this wharf V
I doubt very much if there will be any . revenue from this wharf.

Mr. Chairman, I want to call attention to this point which I gleaned from a statement by the hon. Minister of Public Works. I understand him to say that this is a local matter serving a few people in that neighbourhood. I have no objection at all to it because it is in Nova Scotia, but, I have noticed in other years that the public expenditure has proceeded upon the same lines, not in Nova Scotia alone, but in my own province and, I believe, in all the provinces of the Dominion. I may be wrong, but it appears to me that the practice of expending the money of the Dominion of Canada upon small' undertakings which are in their nature local is not a fair expenditure of the money of the Dominion. It may be a perfectly legitimate expenditure by a province or it may be a perfectly legitimate expenditure by a local municipality. But, unless it serves the interests of Canada as a whole, it is not an honest or judicious expenditure of the moneys of this country. We should not, as a federal parliament, vote the moneys of the people of this country for the promotion of what is merely a local concern. Now, whenever an hon. member of one province opposes an expenditure of this kind, if it is in reference to another province, it is likely to be suggested that he is sectional in his tendencies. But I do so now because this is the first opportunity I have had this session of drawing attention to the matter. I speak of it not in reference to Nova Scotia, but I speak of it in reference to every province of the Dominion, and from my point of view-I do not know what the opinion of the committee is-unless it is shown that there is through traffic to be provided for and that this work in some way will serve the interest of the Dominion as a whole it is not a fair or honest expenditure of the public money and we as a parliament are not justified" in sanctioning the expenditure.

I suppose there is a good deal to be said on both sides of this question. A fine distinction must be drawn to know whether the public interest is being served in each particular locality. On the one hand you have municipal corporations which are wealthy and where the people interested in doing business are wealthy, and a wharf is built at large expenditure to serve the trade of that place, while on the other hand yon have a small place where the people are engaged, as in this instance, in fishing, farm-, ing and that sort of thing and who require wharf accommodation. It has been the policy of the Dominion parliament, probably ever since confederation, to construct these works. I am not prepared at the present moment to make any announcement as to a change of policy. There is no doubt very good service is done the country and that the development of the country is promoted by affording these facilities to the smaller places. We cannot forget that the fishing industry brings a large revenue to the country. It gives employment to a great number of people, although perhaps in an humble way, and it is quite open to discussion whether or not in a locality such as this a small expenditure is not perfectly justifiable. I am not prepared for myself and the government to announce a change of policy at the present moment. Parliament has already approved of these works and I do not think that we would be at liberty to stop their progress. The depth at this point is eleven feet at low water.
There was no discussion on this item last year. I do not know where this place is or anything about it.
I will have to send my hon. friend to school to learn the geography of Nova Scotia.
It would be pretty hard to find in any geography some of the places in Nova Scotia you build wharfs in.
When my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) is Minister of Public Works he will find that he has a good deal of geography to learn. This is situated in Cape Breton county.
Is it let by contract.
This is built by day labour, under the supervision of the government engineer.

Is it the duty of any particular officer to see that the wharfingers all over the country make returns of the revenue received from these wharfs, or whether, as I am informed, there is a rather lax system in regard to this.

The system is that when a wharf has been transferred from the Department of Public Works to the Department of Marine, a wharfinger is appointed and he is bound to make returns and as a rule he does. From some of them there is a very small revenue. The system requires, that returns should be made and I will call the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the statement of my hon. friend.

Is it not the law that where the expenditure is over a certain amount the work has to be let by contract.
THE MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. For eighteen or twenty years in the ease of a work costing less than $5,000 it was supposed that it could be let by an Order in Council without tender. This was found to be ultra vires and now all works are let by tender unless done by day's labour under the department.
It would appear that this wharf cannot be of very great importance because it is three years since we began to vote money for it and it has not yet been commenced.

It has come under my notice that the delay in commencing these public works is sometimes caused by the difficulty in getting a site, and sometimes the estimated cost of the work turns out to be more than the vote and the work is not gone on with until we get a further vote.
Big Pond wharf, $3,100.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Last year $900 was voted for this work, and according to the Audi-
tor General's Report, none of that money was expended. Now we are asked for $2,500.

The $900 was voted last year, but owing to the heavy storms and damage done it was found that it required $2,500 more to renew the superstructure and put it in proper shape. The $900 was spent, .but not having been expended before the 36th of June last, it does not appear in this year's Auditor General's Report.
In what county is this.
Antigonish county.

Are we to understand from the hon. Minister of Public Works that he knows as a matter of fact that a storm swept away this pier and that this accounts for this very large additional amount being required; or are we to understand simply that may be a way for accounting for it ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. My hon. friend has drawn a little on his imagination. I did not say that the pier had been swept away. This is a large wharf, having cost some $35,000. Our information comes from the local engineers who made an estimate of the amount required to put it in repair, and I do not think he would report that it is necessary to repair it unless it is really so.
Bailey's Brook-breakwater wharf, $3,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
There was $2,000 asked for this wharf last year-a new wharf. That was the estimated cost at the time.
I do not see in the Auditor General's Report any account of that $2,000 having been spent. Now my hon. friend asks for $3,000,
I presume to complete the work.

Yes. As none of the $2,000 was spent previous to the 30th of June last, no account of it would appear in the Auditor General's Report of this year. This wharf breakwater is in Pictou county, Nova Scotia, and the estimated cost of the work is $5,000. $2,000 will be spent during the present year and we are asking for $3,000 to complete the work.	.
What is the object of the proposed expenditure ?

This wharf is on the southern shore of Pictou county. It is to provide accommodation for the fishermen and the people in that locality. There was a wharf there previously, but it was very much destroyed, and this expenditure will practically make a new wharf. It is at the mouth of the river, and really acts as a breakwater as well as a landing wharf.

Is the work done by contract or by day labour ?
1Q73
By day labour.
Do we understand that hereafter all new works are to be done by day labour ?

No. In almost every case except repairs and very small works, they are let by public tender. I would not say that in some cases repairs are not let by public tender. The policy of the department is to do most of the repairs and to build some of these small wharfs by day labour under the supervision of the resident engineer; but wherever a wharf can be built by tender, that is done.
Big Pond wharf, $3,100.
Is this for a new structure, or for repairs ?
A new structure. The work has not been commenced. The estimated cost is $3,100.
What is the purpose of it ?
A small wharf is being built for the accommodation of fishermen residing in that district. Their nearest railway station is Grand Narrows1. Freight is iforwarded from that station by steamer.
Is there any anticipated revenue ?

I can hardlyj answer that question. Some of these small wharfs yield quite a revenue and others do not give enough to pay the wharfinger's fees. It is difficult to know until the wharf is built and placed under the jurisdiction of the Marine Department.
The hon. minister can no doubt tell us from his experience in the Marine Department something about the system of returns from these wharfs.

When a wharf is completed it is handed over to the Marine Department and that department finds a wharfinger. In the case of these small wharfs, the wharfinger is generally allowed all the revenue up to $20. Where the revenue is more considerable, the wharfinger receives 25 per cent and makes a regular return to the department according to printed form sent him.
Is this work to be let by contract ?

This is a small work which, will cost altogether $3,100, and will probably be done by day work under the supervision of the government engineer. It is divided up into a great many items and will probably be better done by days' work, under the supervision of the engineer, than by contract.
Would not a small contract like this draw more competition than a large one as there would be more men capable of undertaking it ? In this way the work would likely be done cheaper by contract.

We have to depend a good deal upon the advice of the local engineer. While it might appear to us that it could be done cheaper; by contract, still in places distant from any village, town or settlement, and where the lumber has to be purchased and perhaps floated down during certain seasons of the year, on the whole, taking into account the delays, it would be better to have it done by day work under the supervision of our own engineer.
Is this $3,100 to be the total cost ?

Yes, that is the total estimated cost.
Bridgewater, N.S., dredging, $5,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Why was this money not spent last year ? I see it is a revote.

The department has no dredge to do it, and I am sorry to say there is none to be hired. In a good many places like this, dredging is very much required, and it may be some time before the dredge now under construction may be completed. This is a matter that will have to receive the serious attention of the department.
Is there any chance of getting the ' J. Israel Tarte ' dredge on this work ?
That dredge is doing important work on the St. Lawrence at present.
What preparation is the hon. minister making for increased dredging facilities in Nova Scotia V

There is a large dredge under construction, but I regret that it could not be ready this season. The department will have to seriously consider -what arrangement may be made for the present season as in many of these places dredging is urgently required

I trust the department will look into this matter of dredging very seriously, at once. In a large part of Nova Scotia dredging is absolutely necessary. I have in mind just now one harbour, the harbour of Wallace, where I have been endeavouring for two years to get the department to send a dredge. A part of that harbour is becoming absolutely unnavigable for the want of a small amount of dredging, and it is very important that entrance into the harbour should be improved as a considerable amount of shipping use it. The department would be justified in making

extraordinary efforts to provide increased dredging facilities particularly for tlie harbours in the maritime provinces.

No doubt the province of Nova Scotia is suffering for the want of dredges to do work absolutely necessary. There is a harbour in my county which was deepened in 1882 and on which $82,000 was spent, but which is now beginning- to get shoaly for the want of dredging. During the last two years it has required dredging very badly. We were told by the ex-Minister of Public Works that a new dredge was being built, but from recent inquiries I am afraid it will take as long to build that dredge as it took to build the Temple of Jerusalem.

All those who have followed with some degree of care the shipbuilding that has been going on in the world during the last couple of years, know that material has been very difficult to obtain. Railway men and ship-building men have been unable to get the material they require, and the department, no doubt, has been hampered by the same difficulty. When I left the department a large dredge was well under way at the government shipyard at Sorel, but some time ago I heard that it is not yet completed. I am not surprised, but I fully expected it would be completed in the month of July or August. Of course during the last five months I have not followed up matters in connection with our public works, but that dredge which is under way now in Sorel will have a greater capacity than any of the dredges working in the maritime provinces now. Just as the dredge that bears my name has a greater capacity than nearly all the dredges on the St. Lawrence. That dredge, with the changes that have been made, if I am well informed, will have a capacity of 1,000,000 cubic yards a month. There was never a dredge of that kind built in this country before. The dredge that was intended for the maritime provinces is a suction and also a dipper dredge. It will be a large, sea-going ship. So far, we have imported dredges for the maritime provinces from England. We are now building our own dredges with Canadian hands and on Canadian soil, and, as far as possible we are building them of Canadian material. But, unfortunately, we have not been able, up to this time, to secure Canadian steel plates ; but I hope that the time is not far away when our country will be able to produce the plates. The reason why delays took place while I was in office was that we could not get material. We are not the only ones that have been delayed, however. All the railways, not only in this country, but in the United States, have been hampered in their work because they could not get material. We must take the times as they are- we are in the growing time, in every part of the world. But let me say that the Department of Public Works has built Mr. LOGAN.
a good many dredges during recent years, and it will be necessary to build more, if we wish to grapple with the difficulties and progress with the times. Of course, this country cannot expect to build dredges without providing the money for them. I do not know what my successor's plans are, but I know very well what it is necessary to do in the public interest at this time. We should not hesitate one minute, in my humble opinion in providing all the money that is necessary to equip our waterways in first-class shape.

There are a number of places in Nova Scotia-indeed in all the lower provinces-where, though the members from Ontario and the west may not understand it-it is absolutely necessary that dredging should be done and wharfs built. I have in my mind one instance in a county represented here not by a gentleman supporting the government, but by one on the other side of the House. I refer to the East river in Pictou county. From the harbour at Pictou up to New Glasgow, there are the large works of the Nova Scotia Steel Company. There is need of dredging there. And I trust we shall never assert the rule, that, simply because the county sends a man to support the opposition, therefore no public work shall be done in that county. I understand from those who know that in a number of places in Nova Scotia and in the lower provinces generally dredging can be carried on in winter. In northern Europe, I understand, excellent work is done in dredging during that season. The ice is cut and the material is taken up and put at some distance on the ice. It is carried away by the ice in the spring or sinks at the side of the channel. There are estuaries and rivers in Nova Scotia also, I believe, in Quebec, where work can be done all winter. What can be done elsewhere can be done in Canada, and I am told on very good authority that that work is done in Europe. I am informed that in this way a dredge could be utilized both winter and summer. There are many places where a dredge could not work in winter, for the dredging is carried on in harbours during the fine weather, but when the fall comes and the sea gets rough, nothing can be done. Thus a dredge could work all summer in the harbours, and then, in winter, be taken to East river or some similar place and be utilized all winter. We are only beginning what we have to do in this respect, for we need breakwaters for the security of their boats and we need the dredging in the interests of navigation. I would suggest to the minister that he make inquiries whether or not this winter dredging can be carried on.

I am afraid that it would be very difficult to carry out the suggestion that has been made. My hon. friend

(Mr. Fraser) knows better than I do that most of the harbours in the maritime provinces are very much exposed. Particularly with the dredges that we have to-day, 1 think it would be very difficult to carry on anything of the kind.
I am speaking of rivers.

My experience is that in the months of fall, it is very difficult indeed to get the crews to do any work. In the St. Lawrence river, when November comes it is time to lay up the dredges for a rest. Permit me to say, Mr. Chairman, that it would be in the public interest to equip our country just now, with all the dredges that are necessary. If you look carefully at the reports showing the results of the dredging in the past, you will find that the modern dredges supplied by the government do their work for three or four and five cents a yard, work that, in the past, would have cost twenty-live, forty or fifty cents a yard. The dredge that bears my name, which is the most modern dredge that has been built in this country, during one of the months last season made 600,000 yards in a month. Well, that dredging did not cost much money.
That was working day and night.

Yes. But the dredge has a greater capacity than that. With the changes that have been ordered, the capacity of that dredge is 1,000,000 cubic yards a month. Dredging in so large a quantity, with the same crew of twenty-four men, the cost per cubic yard would be very little indeed. For dredging in the port of St. John, we were asked $1 per cubic yard for dredging, if I remember well. That dredging will not cost us, I am sure, if it is made by one of the government dredges more than five cents or six cents a yard. It is particularly in the public interest to build dredges and to build them in the most modern way. And we must build them without any delay. There is no doubt that we have been late. I do not say that to throw blame on those ministers before me. Now, I may say that when I took office the Department of Public Works had scarcely any dredges worthy of the name. We had only two tubs. It is not then surprising that we are behind the times, that we have many ports that have not been dredged that should have been dredged. But, with the modern implements that we have, with the ship-yard that we have built in Sorel, with many other private ship-yards that we have in Ontario, we can make up for lost time. I would earnestly invite the Minister of Public Works to go on without any hesitation. The country will certainly support him. Our waterways must be equipped now, if we do not want to lose our trade. Our American friends are not losing time. I will not say any more now on this item,
as perhaps we shall have another opportunity to discuss the great question involved.
How much is proposed to be expended on the building of the wharf 1

I can hardly give the hon. gentleman an estimate as to the amount of dredging that may be required at that point. It was thought that $5,000, would do a great deal of useful work in the river, but I do not think it will complete all the dredging that will be required.
Cheverie, breakwater extension, $1,600. '
There was expended in 1901-02, $768, and in the succeeding year, $175. This amount is required to complete the extension. The cost altogether will be $5,243, including the present vote.
What is the necessity of the extension ?
It is an extension into deeper water. It is also used as a landing pier as well as a breakwater.
Why do you make a distinction between a breakwater and a wharf ?
I have never been) able to find out exactly where the distinction is made.

There may be a breakwater and a wharf combined. Suppose you have 200 feet of a breakwater, you build that up with stone until you get out to a certain depth where schooners can come up. Then the stone is covered with cement or wood, so that you can go out upon it just as well as on a wharf. But it serves at the same time as a breakwater for the shipping. It serves as a wharf on which you caul receive goods at the end of it and deliver goods. " Sometimes the wharf is not used at all, because vessels can come inside of the breakwater, which prevent the dashing away of the vessels. But sometimes a breakwater is used to give a certain depth of water to the vessels.
Church Point, repairs to breakwater, $3,000. The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. Last year $1,800 was voted and spent on this work, which will require $3,000 to complete. It is in Digby county.
Has the $1,800 been spent ?

Yes.
Cow Bay (Port Morien),' repairs to breakwater, $25,000.

This was originally built of wood, and the * wood is to be replaced with concrete blocks.

There has been expended on that work, $334,000.
Is this expenditure like those the hon. gentleman and his friends used to accuse us of making, to buy up constituencies with the people's money ?
This is a very old and expensive work. It was built many years ago, and has cost nearly half a million dollars. It will necessarily cost a considerable sum every year if it is to be kept up.
Is it worth the money?
I think it is. There is a large coal mining enterprise carried on in that region, with every promise of great development. I think the country could hardly afford to let the work go down.
I suppose it answers some purpose in connection with coal mining now ?
Tes, the Newcastle Company are operating at that place, it is a service to them. It is a breakwater.
Is that work let by tender, or is it done by day's work ?

I think it is being done by day labour. 260 feet of this breakwater was carried away, and in order to have a permanent work there that would stand the storm, it has been decided to build it with concrete.
Is there any reason why this should not be done by tender and contract ?
It is very difficult to make specifications on which to receive tenders for repairing an old work.
Why should it be difficult ? If it was repairing an old wharf, I could understand it, but here you are providing! for a new breakwater.

This is not a new work. A good deal of that was swept away and we are now going to repair the old pier. As I said, it is difficult to make specifications, because, until the wood work is torn away and uncovered, we do not know how much work will have to be( done. In making the concrete, if it is properly looked after, the work ought to be done as cheaply by day's labour as bv contract.

I did not quite hear the explanation that the hon. minister made when he first was dealing with this matter, but I understand that the $10,000 voted last year has not yet been expended. Is that right ?
Part of it has been expended and the bal- ' ance is now being expended. The estimate of the engineer is that it will be all expended before the 30th June next.

Then I assume that the expenditure has been since the 30th June last, because it is not in the public accounts. That is an expenditure of $10,000 last year and a contemplated expenditure of $25,000 additional this year. This is a very large expenditure. It may be quite justifiable, but it does appear to me that where there is an expenditure of probably $35,000 within two years, the suggestion that the work cannot readily be let by contract does not appear to be reasonable. It may be difficult; all these public undertakings are difficult, more or less, but it is hard to conceive that it is impossible. When it comes to an expenditure so large as this, I think a very serious effort ought to be made to carry out the principle that we are endeavouring to work on in regard to the expenditure of public moneys for large public works in this country, that is, that the work shall be done by tender and contract. Although the hon. minister says that the work to some extent is patching or repairing, I cannot understand why it cannot be done by contract. Both parties to the work would understand it to a large extent. The engineer of the government would understand it on his part, the contractor would be able to estimate it on his part, and it does not appear to me to be a very reasonable ground for departing from what the true intention is, and to say that this work cannot be done by contract. With a work of the magnitude of $25,000 or $30,000 it seems to me it is almost quibbling with the law to say that it cannot properly be done otherwise than by day labour. It is very much like the case of some towns where they have fire limits. When a structure is destroyed you cannot put up a new one unless it comes within the provisions of the fire by-law, but if the structure is only partially destroyed, and you repair it, you may escape the provisions of the by-law. It seems to be a mere distinction in name, because repairs of such an extensive character as to cost $35,000 practically amount to a reconstruction, and they come within the spirit, if not within the letter of the law, which requires public works to be let by tender.

I can hardly agree with the hon. gentleman in regard to a work of this description. This work which is being carried on by day labour would give the department much less trouble if it were let by tender. On the report of the local engineer, approved of by the chief engineer at headquarters, this work is undertaken by day labour, because, in consequence of the peculiarity of the work, they cannot prepare specifications by which it can be let by tender. Any one

who has had any experience of contractors, either in his own business or in connection with the government, will know the great difficulty of letting a work of this kind by contract. It is almost impossible to avoid difficulties and disputes, and when these arise with the contractor, we generally get a good deal the worst of it.-There is not the slightest doubt that owing to the peculiar conditions existing at this particular work it can be much more economically carried on by day labour than by contract. I am not so narrow minded as to say that if there is a community that requires a wharf that because it does not benefit the Dominion as a whole there should not be some expenditure of money, but, in these cases to which I am referring, if the people exported or imported any tiling there must be a revenue and if there is no revenue it is quite evident to any fair minded man that this money was expended when it was really not necessary for the benefit of the community in which the money was expended. I would like an explanation of the fact to clear my mind of suspicion.

I forgot to mention that this is merely the rebuilding of a bridge constructed by the late government supported by hon. gentlemen opposite. The bridge was constructed by the late government and taken over from the provincial government and the municipality. The present government in seeking to vote this money is merely rebuilding the bridge constructed by the late government across that harbour.
I-asked for information and that is no information at all. I was not talking about the bridge.
That happens to be the subject under discussion.

In the province of Ontario a bridge is built across Presque Isle harbour, one of the finest harbours on Lake Ontario, a bridge similar to the one we have under discussion here and it was built by the municipality of Brighton. In the Auditor General's report I find that the revenue of Avonport was $2, which was an in-

crease of seventy-one cents; Bear Point, thirty-four cents; Canada Creek, $2.83; and Cbipman's Brook, $1.20. I might go over a dozen like that and then there are twenty-four from which there is no revenue at all. If the people amongst whom these wharfs are built have anything either to import or export there must be a revenue, and if there is no revenue. it It plain l.o mv inlnT that the wharfs are built at places where they are not necessary.

I may be allowed to explain to my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane), because I know he is in perfect good faith, that I have visited the maritime provinces twice and I have come back with the conviction that the fishermen are a class of men that deserve special attention. We must not expect that they will pay dues for the use of small wharfs we are building. They are carrying on a large and profitable trade for the Dominion, and it is because I acquired that belief after having visited the maritime provinces, that I am responsible for the very many wharfs that appear today in these estimates. If my hon. friend would give himself the pleasure of visiting the maritime provinces he would appreciate the importance of these works. The fishermen are carrying on a most profitable trade for the Dominion and they deserve to be encouraged. When my friends on the other side [DOT]will be in power they will build wharfs as the present government is building them to-day. This is not a party question by any means ; it is a large public question and I invite my hon. friend (Sir. Cochrane) to think twice over what I have said in my very humble way, before condemning that expenditure of money.

Nova Scotia seems to be well served in this matter. There are fishermen in my own constituency who have paid their licenses for years and have never received any assistance to improve their harbours. In fact, they have had to find the money for that out of their own pockets.
On several occasions votes have been placed in the estimates without the department having full information as to the cost of the work to be carried out ; and I must say that that is so in this case.
Why should it be so ?

It is a little difficult to say why, to be frank. Petitions are put in asking for works, and then a certain amount is placed in the estimates. Any man who has passed through the Department of Public Works knows that we have so many works that it is quite impossible to have surveys in every case.
Some hon. gentlemen from Nova Scotia may go back to their constituencies and say that the opposition is objecting to all these items. We don't object to these improvements, but we object to the system pursued by the government, which keeps the House in the dark as to what the ultimate cost of these works will be.

I agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) but he must remember that in no case to-night were we unable to estimate almost in detail the total cost of any work we asked a vote for. I hope in future to stick to that rule. There may be exceptions to every rule, but so far as I am concerned, I think it is a good rule, and I shall have a report and an estimate made on every work for which we ask a vote when that is possible. It is quite probable that it may take more than one year to do certain works, but 1 believe that the House should be in possession of full information as to what the probable cost of a work will be before we undertake it.

They applied for $1,000 or $2,000 to enable their boats to go in and out of the harbour, but they were refused. I myself have applied to the Marine Department and was refused and told to go to the Public Works Department. The government issue licenses to the fishermen and if they can render the harbours serviceable at a reasonable cost they are doing right in making these expenditures. But what we complain of is that the government puts an item in the estimates the first year and then for several years afterwards they come down asking more money for the same work. That is not right. When we pass an appropriation here to commence a work we should know the full cost of that work so that we may understand what we are doing. The system of applying for these works is either by petitioning the department, or get-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We are pursuing the rather unusual course here of voting money for a bridge, and I would ask my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. McLennan) who is conversant with this matter, if this is a swing bridge.
There is a draw on this bridge.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend stated that tliis bridge was originally constructed by the late government. In what year was the money voted for it.
The money was voted in 1895 and it was built in 1896.

The hon. gentleman lias treated this as a bridge over a natural channel, and he cited the case of a bridge in Ontario which was constructed

over a harbour, aiul where the municipality had to build it. I do not understand that in that case there was auy interference with the natural conditions. In this case the Dominion government for its own purpose in making a harbour, cut through the public highway and rendered a bridge necessary where there was no bridge required before, or perhaps only a small culvert. If the Dominion government had not touched the place there would be no necessity for the local authorities to put in a costly bridge at all. But if the Dominion government cut through the public highway and made a waterway across, then there was the same reason why the Dominion government should build a bridge over that as they would over a canal. I happen to know something about this, because I was in the government of Nova Scotia when the question was raised between the Dominion and local authorities as to who should build that bridge, and after full discussion, it was concluded that inasmuch the need for the bridge was caused by the construction by the Dominion government of what was practically a canal, they were as much obliged to provide a bridge over that waterway as they would be to provide a bridge over a canal in any part of Ontario. That is the principle upon which this bridge was constructed by the Dominion government.

Iam not quite satisfied about this bridge yet. This is called a pond, but we have many of these ponds in the maritime provinces which may be called harbours, and this bridge at the entrance to this pond is going to cost $1,500 for repairs. I cannot yet see for the life of me why the people of Canada should pay for the building of a bridge to the entrance of that pond. I have known cases in Prince Edward Island where the Dominion government by deepening the water have caused the local authorities great expense to build bridges to accommodate the travelling public. This is merely an ordinary traffic bridge. It is simply a local bridge. A good deal has been said with regard to the amount expended in Nova Scotia for these public works. I have no fault to find with that expenditure. I speak in no carping spirit of the money spent on these improvements, and I can appreciate the needs of the fishermen of Nova Scotia in prosecuting their precarious industry, but we have a right to have these matters fully discussed in parliament, and when we find the public money is being diverted from its proper use, to have it explained by the government.

Do I understand the Minister of Finance to say that the channel which this bridge covers was excavated by the Dominion government ? What does pond mean ? In our section of the country it means a body of still water. Is it utilized for a harbour ?
This channel was constructed into a harbour.
What was it before V

There was no navigable channel before.
Green Cove-boat harbour, $6,600.

Will the minister explain this ?
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) That work is in the county of Victoria, and is now under contract. The object is to have a harbour for the shelter of fishermen's boats.
The total cost of this work is $G,G00. It is now under contract. The amount of the contract is $6,275.

What sized boats will it accommodate ?
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Sailing boats belonging to the fishermen who go out quite long distances from the shore when the navigation opens, and continue till the fall of the year. Formerly they could not use larger boats because they had to haul them up in stormy weather. When this is built, the boats will be comfortably moored from tlie beginning of the fishing season till the fall of the year.

Will it enable the fishermen to use larger boats ?
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Yes, that is the object of it.
Mi\ BLAIN. What system of collecting these small amounts from wharfs do the government adopt ? Have they officials for that purpose ?

Whenever a wharf is completed and turned over to the Marine Department, they appoint a wharfinger who collects the fees and turns them over to the department. In the case of these small wharfs which are built to provide shelter for fishermen, I doubt very much if fees are collected. In some cases wharfs are not turned over to the Marine Department, but are kept under the control of the Department of Public Works.
For instance, at Avonport, there was a revenue last year of $2. How would that be collected ?
It would be collected by a wharfinger.
What salary would be paid to the wharfinger ?
The general rule is to allow the wharfinger 25 per cent of the receipts.
My impression is that where the collections do

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: not reach the amount which the wharfinger is to be paid for his services, he is not obliged to make a return, and that may be the reason why some of these wharfs do not appear to pay any fees. I would not be positive as to that, but even in such cases I think the wharfinger ought to make a return to show what he receives and what he keeps. That is worth looking into.
I notice a number of wharfs returning from 37 cents up to $2. Can the minister tell us how these fees were collected, and what percentage of salary was paid to the persons who made the collections ?

That is information to be obtained from the Marine Department. There is no doubt that the small return made to the department is the amount over and above the salary or percentage allowed to the wliarf-. inger for collecting the fees and attending to the wharf.
1-Ie may or he may not.
That may be the net revenue after paying his fees. I will look into that.
What are the duties of a wharfinger ?
To take care of the wharf and collect the wharfage rates.
What do you mean by taking care of the wharf ?
Ills chief duty would be to see that every person who used the wharf would pay a proper wharfage rate. He would also see that no damage was done to the wharf.

I agree with the Minister of Finance that in any case there should be a return made of the amount collected. When there is no return, you may assume that the wharfinger has not collected the amount of his remuneration, but you have no guarantee of that.
What is understood by a boat harbour ? I understand that it means a harbour for fishermen ?
Yes.

It would be convenient if that term were applied to all these harbours which are built solely for fishermen, so that when we came to them we would not expect any revenue. In several eases to-night we were told that a wharf was necessary. As I said before, I am prepared to vote the money if it is necessary, but it must be necessary for importing or
exporting something, and if so there must be some revenue. Does the wharfinger take any of the receipts of the wharf for repairs?
Not Without special order.

If the wharf is necessary for the people in order to serve in the export for their commodities and the import of what they require, there must be a revenue from it, and that would appear in the Auditor General's Report. If there is no revenue then the wharf is not necessary or the wharfinger is pocketing the money.
Hawk Point Inlet, N.S., boat channel, $1,000.

This is to permit a larger class of boats going in than now pass through. This will complete the work.
Herring Cove, breakwater, $9,800.
By tender, I suppose ?

Yes, the work is let to the lowest tenderer. It is in Halifax county.
Janvrin's Island wharf, $2,000.
Is this a new work ?
Yes, the total estimated cost is $2,000.
Has anything been done up to this time ? It appears to have been standing some years and nothing spent.
No, nothing has been spent.
What is the idea of voting this year after year and not spending the money ?
A considerable number of votes were taken for small works down in that province and the engineer in charge with his staff has not been able to look after them all.
It is not very pressing.
Tlie people there seem to think it is important. I shall try and see that it is attended to during the next few months.
What year was the first vote taken ?
I have not the records.
Was it before the last election ?
The vote was taken last year.
I think the kon. gentleman is mistaken. If he will look at the estimates he will find that it was taken before last year.

No, last year was the first time this vote was taken.
Judique, repairs, &c., to breakwater, $400.
What is the total cost ?
Kingsport, reconstruction of pier, $3,000.
What is the necessity for this ?

This is a government breakwater which was constructed some twenty or thirty years ago and on which probably $30,000 of Dominion money has been expended. A year ago last autumn, as the result of a very severe gale, a portion of the pier was injured very seriously, and this money is for the purpose of repairs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: How long is the pier ?
About 500 feet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What proportion was torn down or blown away ?

The upper portion of the pier was twisted over down to within a few feet of the bottom. It is a tidal pier and when the tide is out it is dry land,* but there is about thirty feet of water when the tide is in. This storm came while the tide was in, and tin; force of the waves carried probably forty or fifty feet of the end of the pier over.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Will this put it in good shape and be all the money required ?
The engineer estimates that this will complete the work and put it in good shape.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I see by the Auditor General's Report that last year there was expended on this work $9,208.70 and now we are asked to spend another $4,000. On page V-208 I find that Mr. Alfred Totter was conductor for 181 days at $2.50 per day and that Mr. Eben Cox was foreman for sixty-four days at $2.50 a day. I notice that on all these constructions of piers and wharfs there is a conductor at $2.50 or $3 per day, but in this case there were both a conductor and a foreman at $2.50 per day-and all for an expenditure of $9,000. What are their respective duties ?
The conductor is the man who buys the material and generally conducts the' work. The foreman of construction is a mechanic who sees that the work is done properly by the men engaged.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How much will the work cost altogether ?
The total cost will be $41,790.
One would suppose that a practical man could both superintend the work and buy the material. That is merely a suggestion. Perhaps, for some reason he cannot do it.

In some circumstances, that might be so. But this is a considerable work, and if he went away to look after material, leaving no one to take charge of the men, it might not be an economical arrangement.
What is it built of ?
Timber.
In our section to do work with timber economically we would have the timber cut in the water, when it could be hauled cheaply and then built in the summer.
That was done with many works.
Then, you would not need two men. One man capable of buying timber would also see that the work was done.

There are two men named, but they are not both on all the time.
Larry's river, breakwater, $14,250.
This work is under contract. The amount being $15,840. The contractors are Reid & Archibald, of Halifax.
What is this work and what constituency is it in ?
In my constituency. This is a small fair harbour. Two years ago there came a terrific storm by which the mouth of the harbour was filled up.
With suckers ?
No, largely with rocks. The people there own quite a number of schooners, and this vote is to make a breakwater.
How many schooners ?
I do not know how many- but quite a number of schooners ply between there and Halifax and go to the fishing grounds. This is a very necessary work.
What did the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser) do in order to get the department to undertake this work ?
Nothing, except to ask them to send the engineer. The need of the work was so apparent that the engineer reported in favour of it'without another word from me.
Will the hon. gentleman say what time the engineer reported ?
I think it was last year.
Before the session of parliament ?
I am not sure of the date of my report. The first vote was given last session.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser) will refer to page 1002 of last year's ' Hansard ' he will see that the hon. minister says there was no report.

There may have been no report at that time. The engineer was there. But I may say about the engineers in Nova Scotia-and I am speaking in the presence of the hon. minister-that last year I think I had four reports to be made in my county, and one of them is not made yet. The engineers have so little help, at least that is what they say, that they do not make reports. They were ordered to make this report before the vote. There was a report came in before any contract was made.

That is what we complain of on this side-that the department was induced to put a sum in the estimates last year without a report, for the minister was asked what the probable cost would be and he said he had no idea, for there was no estimate to show. Now, lion, gentlemen opposite can quite understand that we are justified in complaining about estimates so made. This is not a business way for a business administration to do-to bring down votes without preparing an estimate, so that both sides may know what they are doing.
Lingan, beach protection, $1,000.
Why is this money asked this year for this work ?
This makes a total of $1,600 for this work- $600 last year and $1,000 this year. This is brush and stone work, to repair damage made in beach protection work.
But we were told that the $600 voted last year would complete the work.
This damage may have occurred during the interval. It may be that the $600 is for repairs then required, but that since then the necessity has arisen for spending this money.
The hand of Providence seems to have been very hard on these works.
It does seem to have been stormy in Nova Scotia.
But there must be some reasonable excuse for this vote if it is worthy of our consideration.

In all seriousness, what is this vote for ? What do we understand
by * beach protection ?' There must be something inside the beach in which the public is interested in order to justify this work.

As I understand it, these are small natural "harbours which are injured by the waves of the seas, and, to protect them, brush and stone are put down to make a shelter to protect the points of beach from washing away. It is much cheaper than building wharfs.
So this is to protect some point that might otherwise be washed away ?

Fes.
Lunenburg, dredging harbour, $5,000.

This is a revote of a sum that has been standing in the estimates for a number of years-and why it should be there, without being appropriated, I cannot understand. My friends say it is to please the people. My own opinion is that they would be better pleased with a vote of this kind if it were expended. I was told last year it was for the want of a proper dredge to do that work, as a lai'ge amount of work had to be done. The government is right in saying it is an immense work for it is required for the benefit of the shipping of these ports. I speak without boasting when I say that the ports of Lunenburg and Bridgewater are two of the most important ports in the whole province. Lunenburg owns a larger amount of shipping than the whole of Halifax. Bridgewater has a very large amount of shipping also, and of heavier tonnage going in and out of that port. And why both of these ports should be hampered in the way, and that for years for want of a proper dredge to do the dredging, I can not understand. The Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Finance were at these ports three or four years ago. They came in a steamer measuring about fifty tons.
They happened to be there at low tide, and had they remained fifteen minutes longer they would have been compelled to remain until the return of the tide, some twelve hours. The boat turned up the mud as they went out of the harbour, so shallow was the water near the pier, and that shallowness of water extended all over the harbour. The banks of the harbour are alluvial, and the wash from the repeated rains carry the debris into the harbour and fill it up from year to year. Now to show the necessity for that dredging, I will say that last year, had we not used smaller vessels, we would have been deprived of the opportunity of importing salt from across the ocean in large steamers for the want of a sufficient depth of water. We are compelled to confine ourselves strictly to smaller vessels in order to bring in that
comioxs
nos
supply. The shallowness of water also deprives us of the industry of ship building of heavy tonnage. This year we built something like thirty odd vessels of a fair size, averaging from one hundred to three hundred and fifty tons, and they require a considerable depth of water to float them.' Now these amounts have been In the estimates for a long time, and has not been expended, I would ask when is this going to end ? By delay they are discouraging the industry of shipbuilding. I venture to say that the coming year there will scarcely be any vessels built, for they will not be able to come into those ports on account of shallow water. When that industry of shipbuilding is interfered with the consequence is an interference with the industry of the woodsman supplying the timber and the carpenters as well engaged in construction. It interferes largely also with the traders.
Now, when told last year that for the want of a dredge this money was not expended in either Bridgewater or Lunenburg, I took it for granted that I had an Indirect promise that dredges were being built, and that in a little while these dredges would be in service, and would be placed at work in those two ports. A dredge was built, as I understand, and has been in use the past year. Will the Minister of Public Works say that there has been no dredge in Nova Scotia during the past year ? I do not think he can say so, for I have learned that a lot of dredging has been done during the past year; but why Lunenburg and Bridgewater should be overlooked and other ports of less consequence cared for, I cannot for the life of me understand. I am here to! represent the interests of the people, and I claim that work as a right. I feel satisfied that the government are doing themselves a serious injury, they are injuring the industry of ship-building, and are indirectly hurting other industries as well by not giving us those dredges. Bridgewater requires a large amount of dredging, because it is a navigable river for about twenty miles. The bar requires dredging as weil as the upper parts of the river, where there has been a large amount of sawdust deposited as well as refuse from the banks of the river. But I ask the minister in all seriousness that he will not look upon this request as of small moment, but that he will give it the recognition it deserves. I hope that this year dredges will be placed in service at Lunenburg and Bridgewater and Mahone Bay, and I feel satisfied that if the minister will consider the case for a moment, he will be convinced of the absolute necessity of this work, unless he wants to stop the navigation of those waters entirely.

We passed a similar item to-night with regard to an appropriation for Bridgewater. We pass these appropriations from year to year and still we have no assurance that any work will be undertaken this year any more than it has Mr. KAULBACH.
been done in the past. I think we should have some assurance from the Minister of Public Works that something will be done, that these harbours will be dredged. It seems to be useless to pass these votes from year to year without we have an understanding from the Minister of Public Works that some progress will be made.
Mr. IvAULBACH. I am waiting for an answer from the Minister of Public Works with respect to the request that I have made for an expenditure at those two ports.

Before my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works answers, I want to say a word on the subject myself. If the presence of this vote in the estimates is offensive to my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach), we will get over that matter very easily by striking it out. When he alluded a moment ago to the policy of keeping this vote on the book in order to deceive the people, and so forth, if he is serious, I think we will accommodate him by striking it out. But I venture to say that if we did strike it out he would be the first to complain, and to ask why we did not revote it. It is a fact that all along the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia \ve are experiencing difficulties in the matter of dredging. We have one or two little dredges of an inferior pattern which are doing a little work, but we are not weil equipped with dredging plant. In the case of the great lakes, where the government have no dredges available, it is sometimes found possible to hire private dredges. We are willing to hire dredges for the coast of Nova Scotia if they could be found. When I interested myself in the matter, and asked the late Minister of Public Works to make an inquiry whether we could obtain dredges, I know he did make an inquiry, and he was not able to obtain dredges from any quarter. They are not to be found, they are not available. We are now building a couple of dredges, but they are large works, and the construction proceeds slowly. But as soon as these dredges are completed, we hope that some of these important works can be attended to ; but if we cannot get the dredges, if we cannot hire them or get them constructed in a short time, then it would be useless for us to make a promise to my hon. friend that we will do this work. I am as anxious as he is to have the work done. I appreciate the importance of Lunenburg and Bridgewater, and I heartily agree with him that Lunenburg is the most important point on the whole coast as regards the deep sea fishing industry. I sympathize heartily with him, but I do not think his case was as urgent as some other cases, for Lunenburg has a fine harbour. It is beginning to suffer, and I appreciate his desire that it should be dredged. If dredges are used in some other cases, it is because the work for the moment seemed more urgent. There are some cases

where the work was more urgent for the moment, though not of more importance. Then with respect to Bridgewater particularly, there is no dredge that we have in the maritime provinces which is at all suitable for that work. If it is a question of transferring a dredge from one place to another, I am sure that I am correct in stating in the hearing of the late Minister of Public Works and of the present minister and of the engineers of the department, that we have not a dredge in the lower provinces which is capable of doing the work at Bridgewater. We do not want to withdraw the vote, my hon. friend would not desire us to do so. Even though we are not in a position to guarantee the doing of the work, we leave it there as an evidence of good faith ; and if we can buy, or build, or hire dredges, we are as anxious as lie is that this work and other works along the coast of Nova Scotia shall be provided for.
What is the depth of water at Lunenburg ?

At low tide it would be little more than nine feet, and our smallest schooners draw that amount of water. In regard to the remarks of the hon. gentleman, I know he is inclined to be generous, but, still at the same time, I did not like to hear a remark made by him in regard to the withdrawal of the vote.
I do not think my hon. friend is serious in pressing it.

I did not refer to it in any disingenious way at all. If there is any difficulty in obtaining dredges for work of that description I will ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if he will permit me to get parties to construct dredges and place them at the service of the government at a certain rate per cubic yard. If so, I will be prepared to get parties to construct dredges that will do all the dredging required.

I know the hon. Minister of Public Works does not hear my hon. friend's question as he is engaged in conversation at the present moment, and under these circumstances I will presume to answer it. I think my hon. friend is mistaken when he says that he can obtain dredges so readily. The construction of a modern dredge is not by any means so simple a matter as some suppose. I do not think my hon. friend can get any dredges, but if he knows anybody who has a dredge available and suitable to the work along the Atlantic coast and would place that party in communication with the hon. Minister of Public Works I am quite sure he will have ample employment at dredging at fair and reasonable rates. As to the particular places to which the dredge should go first, I am sure my hon. friend will agree
with me that while he mentioned Lunenburg and Bridgewater they are not the only places that are complaining. If he knows anybody who is prepared to place a dredge at the disposal of the government on the Atlantic coast at a fair and reasonable rate, I am quite sure he will have an ample opportunity for employment.

I am not anxious to encourage the introduction of dredges from across the border, but I can get dredges in the United States that will go to work in the course of a very little while and do the work necessary at so much per cubic yard and I think it can be done quite as cheaply as by constructing dredges by the government and employing parties to do the work. I do not approve of going across the border and bringing workmen or dredges here, but at the same time, I approve of the government insisting that this work shall be completed at the earliest possible moment.
I think it is really unconstitutional to go into supply at all on Mondays but I have not objected to It. We had better stop now.

I am pleased with the progress we have made and I shall be glad to meet the views of the Committee.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved the adjournment of the House.
There were some papers to be brought down in connection with the Redistribution Bill-correspondence with the government of New Brunswick.
I have the correspondence here but it is in such shape that I would hardly like to put it on the Table of the House. I will have it arranged and bring it down to-morrow.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: What business will we take up to-morrow ?
We may take several bills including, I think, the Rt. Hon. Prime Minister intended, the Redistribution Bill for the second reading, and if we get beyond that, Supply.
The Rt. Hon. Prime Minister mentioned that matter to me personally. I do not know whether we will have these documents down sufficiently early to enable us to go on with the Redistribution Bill.
Did my hon. friend mention it to the Prime Minister ?
I did, and he said that if any difficulty of that kind arose lie would not insist upon it.
Whatever arrangement the hon. gentleman has made with the Prime Minister will be carried out. In that case we may take some of the Bills on the Order Paper and then supply.

We really want to look at this correspondence before the second reading, because, if any discussion arises in regard to this matter, it will be on the second reading. Therefore, we should have these documents a reasonable length of time beforehand. I hardly think at present we will be justified in going on with the discussion to-morrow.
If my hon. friend has had an understanding with the Prime Minister I have nothing to add. It will be carried out.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
Tuesday, April 7, 1903.
